title: A Pre-registered, Cryptographically Timestamped Proving Protocol for Directional Market Forecasting, with Announced Echo State Network and Quantum Reservoir Computing Examinations
abstract: Directional forecasting claims about markets are, in common practice, unfalsifiable: the search behind a published strategy is unreported, the benchmark is chosen alongside the results, and failed attempts leave no record. We present a proving protocol that makes such claims checkable without trusting the authors. Every evaluative decision is committed to a cryptographically timestamped append-only record before it can be compared with outcomes. We report the protocol's first completed application: a baseline stage across five market target streams, in which four model paradigms — from regularized linear models to a large language model — all failed to exceed floors set by a pre-registered naive family operating on price alone, net of costs. The floors, the statistical machinery (a cumulative hypothesis family under Romano-Wolf stepdown control, validated on synthetic ground truth), and the enforcement patterns that make protocol violations machine-detectable or impossible by construction are published in full. On this record we announce, in registered-report form, the project's next examinations: an echo state network stage, and a quantum reservoir stage evaluated as the symmetric difference ∆ against an exactly twinned classical arm. To our knowledge this is the first pre-registered forward test of quantum reservoir computing against a matched classical counterpart in financial forecasting. The design invariants are timestamped with this paper; the full designs undergo registered-report review before any run. Their outcomes, and the per-arm grid of the baseline stage, are published in a separate results report under the disclosure policy fixed here, whatever the sign of ∆.
why: All forecasting models fail pre-registered protocol, net costs.

title: Does Empirical Finance Replicate?
abstract: An autonomous LLM pipeline rebuilds each result from the paper and available databases, with independent audits of every replication. I obtain 1,328 in-sample replications, 1,005 with enough post-sample data for an out-of-sample test. In sample, 75% reproduce the published sign and significance, and the median coefficient recovers 0.93 of the published value. Out of sample, the rate falls to 42%, and the median coefficient ratio to 0.45. The coefficient ratio drops sharply when the original sample ends and is flat on either side, consistent with data snooping rather than investor learning or gradual market change. Although original t-statistics strongly predict persistence, standard models of publication selection explain only about one-fifth of the overall decay. Published finance is largely reproducible in its original samples but much less durable in later data.
why: 42% out-of-sample survival rate shatters replication claims; career-changing for practitioner skepticism.

title: Point-in-Time SEC Financial Data: A Reproducible Benchmark for Detecting Look-Ahead and Restatement Leakage
abstract: Historical financial research can fail before a return series is joined. A database may attach a fact to its fiscal period end, retain only the latest comparative value, or continue serving a number after an issuer has withdrawn reliance on the underlying financial statements. Each design can place information into a historical decision that was not admissible at that time. This paper presents the AhaSignals Financial AI Point-in-Time Integrity Benchmark v1.1, an openbook, deterministic conformance suite built from accession-level U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings. The benchmark contains eight purposively selected cases, five issuers, four failure families and sixteen prompts across evidence-restricted retrieval and knowledgecontamination tracks. It uses SEC acceptance timestamps as an auditable regulatory event clock and requires the tested system to cite the controlling accession, exclude later filings, preserve evidence-state changes and abstain during a non-reliance interval. A deliberately contaminated calibration response is rejected as a temporal-integrity failure. In one AhaSignals-operated pilot, a financial AI system returned sixteen conforming responses, with no temporal-integrity failures; this is an execution-chain result, not a general model ranking. In the studied CoreWeave source set, a latest-value query replaces all fourteen matched facts in an earlier decision set and reverses the sign of one reported value. A BigBear.ai ledger preserves 160 non-zero issuerlabelled corrections across the previously reported, non-reliance and restated states. These are deterministic case results, not market-frequency estimates. The contribution is a small, fully auditable test of whether a financial system obeys the information clock before it computes a factor or backtest.
why: Reproducible benchmark for look-ahead bias, directly useful practitioners.

title: A Thousand Agents, One Opinion: Effective Population Collapse in LLM-based Artificial Markets
abstract: Agent-based finance established that the variety of agents' forecasts is what separates calm markets from bubbles. The field is now rebuilding those markets out of language models, where every agent is the same base model under a different prompt-and where the training procedure that makes a model usable as an agent is known to reduce output diversity. We show what this costs. If agents' belief vectors share a fraction ρ of their variance, the effective population is N_eff = N/[1 + (N-1)ρ], which cannot exceed 1/ρ for any N: a market of a million agents with ρ = 0.3 has the aggregate-belief variability of 3.3 independent traders. Aggregate excess-demand variance is inflated by exactly 1 + (N-1)ρ, an identity we verify to within 1.46% across fifteen configurations, and the single shared draw supplies most of the market's average belief as soon as ρ > 1/(N + 1)-one per cent at N = 100. Sampling temperature cannot repair this: the correlation floor is σ_b²/(σ_b² + σ_w²), so N_eff ≤ 1 + σ_w²/σ_b² regardless of N. In a full adaptive-belief market the dynamic consequence lies in the microstructure: monoculture leaves median volatility without systematic dependence on ρ but erodes volatility clustering from acf(|r|,1) = 0.224 to 0.127 (-44%) and deepens the negative volumevolatility relation from-0.139 to-0.293, because aligned beliefs produce one-sided books. We then measure ρ directly on prompted language-model agents: sixteen agents, 60 shared real market states, 10,560 forecasts. A population drawn from one aligned model has ρ@ = 0.341 and an effective size of 2.6 out of sixteen. Adding distinct personas does not help and slightly hurts (0.255 → 0.341), so the literature's main instrument for creating heterogeneity does not create it. Alignment is a large part of the cause: the base checkpoint of the same model at the same size gives ρ@ = 0.098 and N_eff = 6.5, so post-training raises the shared component 3.5-fold. The one effective remedy is drawing agents from different base models, which lowers ρ@ to 0.145; a withinversus-between decomposition confirms the mechanism is genuinely different priors (-0.101, 95% CI [-0.145,-0.065]). Those measured populations then trade: 110 of them across 2,200 independent markets. Cross-market dispersion of volatility falls with the measured effective population (p = 0.0001), and the nominal agent count adds nothing once the effective one is known-N alone explains R² = 0.006 of the variation against 0.126 for N_eff, and adding N to a model containing N_eff is indistinguishable from noise (p = 0.30). We therefore propose that LLM-agent market studies report the measured cross-agent forecast correlation and the implied effective population alongside the agent count, and give the protocol for doing so.
why: Quantifies agent collapse formula, empirically verified configurations.

title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly 'reason' with increasing sophistication, but whether they 'know' when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning-Kruger-like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence-accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning systems.
why: LLM overconfidence on finance reasoning, thirty models tested.

title: When LLMs Whisper: Information Leakage and Collusion in Financial Markets
abstract: LLMs used for trading emit reasoning traces opaque to humans but parsable by other LLMs. How does this hidden channel reshape tacit collusion in financial markets? I embed pre-trade leakage in a market with informed traders and a competitive market maker. Leakage sharpens posteriors about fundamental value and renders the rival's intended order predictable. Both channels (information and enforcement) relax the repeated-game incentive constraint and expand the sustainable-collusion set. Q-learning and production-LLM experiments verify the mechanism; mitigation is explored. The analysis suggests LLM deployment can expand the sustainablecollusion frontier; welfare cost falls hardest where price-based monitoring is weakest.
why: LLM reasoning traces enable market collusion; market-structure insight tested with Q-learning. Practitioner should know risk.

title: Etemaro: An LLM Agent with Federated Experiential Learning for Autonomous Concentrated-Liquidity Management on Solana
abstract: Concentrated liquidity market makers (CLMMs), such as Meteora's Dynamic Liquidity Market Maker (DLMM) on Solana, require liquidity providers to continuously select pools, size discrete bin ranges, and time entries and exits. This constitutes a sequential decision problem under partial observability that static, parametric rebalancing vaults (e.g., Kamino Finance, 2024; Gamma Strategies) handle poorly in volatile, high-turnover markets. Conversely, recent large language model (LLM) trading agents (e.g., FinMem (Yu et al., 2023), FinAgent (Zhang et al., 2024)) focus predominantly on isolated single-agent spot or perpetual trading, lacking domain-specific bin mechanics and cross-instance knowledge sharing. We present Etemaro, an autonomous architecture that utilizes an LLM inside a ReAct reasoning loop to screen candidate pools, deploy and manage DLMM positions, and execute exits based on live profit-and-loss, yield, and bin drift data. Etemaro introduces three primary contributions beyond standard trading-agent frameworks: (1) a Darwinian signal-weighting mechanism that reweights heuristic screening signals online using a quartile-lift statistic computed from realized win/loss outcomes; (2) role-scoped and intent-filtered tool access, strictly constraining which on-chain actions the LLM may execute across screening, management, and chat contexts; and (3) HiveMind, a lightweight federated experiential-learning protocol where independent agent instances exchange natural-language lessons and scored strategy presets without sharing raw transaction logs, private keys, or model weights. We evaluate Etemaro through a continuous 114-day production deployment on Solana Mainnet (April 1 to August 24, 2026). Across this period, the agent executed 4,583 on-chain deployments committing 9,715.52 SOL in capital (~2.12 SOL average per position) and generated 50,329 on-chain lifecycle events, achieving a 68.35% realized win rate (743 wins out of 1,087 closed positions) with a median hold time of 36.5 minutes. We candidly document operational failure modes, including a 37.25% state divergence between local logs and on-chain reality caused by RPC dropouts and 5,521 concurrent race-condition transactions. We position this work as a systems and architecture contribution, establishing an empirical template for safety-constrained, self-improving autonomous agents operating in live financial environments. Overall, our findings demonstrate that combining bounded reasoning loops with lightweight experiential federation enables autonomous agents to operate effectively and self-adaptively in high-velocity decentralized financial markets.
why: Real LLM trading problem, no visible results or implementation evidence.

title: Cost-efficient SME Credit Assessment with Machine Learning: A Calibration-centered Comparison of PD Models
abstract: SME credit risk assessment remains costly for lenders, and probability of default (PD) models are the standard instrument for reducing that cost without sacrificing lending quality. Comparing such models on 4,580 SME cases with a 4.3 percent default rate, we find that logistic regression with Weight of Evidence transformation, calibrated Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM and their equal-weight ensemble deliver comparable discrimination once every metric is measured 5-fold out-of-fold with the full pipeline refitted inside each fold. With all five models within 0.04 Gini of one another (0.55 to 0.59), discrimination alone cannot differentiate them; calibration quality and interpretability become the deciding criteria. The study documents three findings the discrimination-focused literature underemphasizes. First, SMOTE resampling in a properly constructed pipeline shapes only intermediate artefacts and leaves every deployed probability unchanged. Second, calibration has a level and a shape requiring different instruments: the natural default rate sets the level, while cross-fitted beta calibration corrects the shape, removing the probability floor imposed by averaged fold-calibrators and moving Random Forest and XGBoost from failing the Hosmer-Lemeshow test to passing it, at a cost of 0.011 Gini. Third, evaluation paths that refit preprocessing on evaluation data inflate results, here by 0.09 Gini for the logistic regression. The article closes with model selection guidance, a rating scale and a validation sequence for institutions balancing performance with supervisory expectations.
why: Methodologically sound but standard ML without novelty.

title: Faithfulness Under Pressure: Evaluating Hallucination Detectors for Financial RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used in financial applications where generated answers must be grounded in specific documents, filings, or disclosures. Yet even with relevant context, answers may contradict, overextend, or misinterpret the supplied evidence. This paper presents a comparative study of intrinsic hallucination detection for financial RAG, where the task is to determine whether an answer is faithful to a supplied question-context pair. We evaluate DSPy-based prompt optimization, fine-tuned detectors, encoder-based detectors, and LLM-as-Judge frameworks across public benchmarks and finance-specific settings. To examine finance-specific behavior, we construct FinDER-HD, a balanced hallucination-detection benchmark derived from FinDER by synthesizing unfaithful counterparts for faithful financial question-context-answer examples. We further evaluate filing-scale robustness on PHANTOM, which varies context length, evidence position, and filing type. Results show that detector performance varies substantially across datasets, financial topics, reasoning types, and context regimes. DSPy-based prompt optimization is competitive under limited supervision, but robustness differs markedly by optimization strategy: demonstration-heavy methods perform strongly in short contexts yet degrade more sharply as context grows, whereas COPRO and especially GEPA remain substantially more stable. Selected LLM-as-Judge methods also perform strongly in finance-specific settings, but their operating behavior depends on threshold choice and prediction bias. These findings motivate deployment-oriented evaluation of financial RAG guardrails beyond aggregate F1, including finance-specific robustness, filing-scale stress testing, prediction bias, threshold calibration, and contextwindow feasibility.
why: Useful hallucination detection evaluation for RAG but infrastructure not core financial problem.

title: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks for Money Laundering Detection in Bitcoin Transaction Graphs
abstract: Money laundering on public blockchains is difficult to detect because the evidence is spread thinly across many ordinary looking transfers. Most published detectors treat the Bitcoin ledger as a single homogeneous graph in which every edge carries the same meaning. That assumption discards information, since a payment edge, a spending edge, a shared input relation and a temporal succession edge say different things about intent. This paper presents BitHGN, a heterogeneous graph neural network that keeps these relations separate, learns one message transform per relation using a basis decomposition, and then fuses the relation specific messages through a learned semantic attention weight. The model encodes the discrete time step of every transaction and is trained with a focal objective together with a logit adjustment term, because only about two percent of the labelled nodes are illicit. Experiments use the publicly available Elliptic Data Set distributed on Kaggle, which contains 203,769 transaction nodes, 234,355 directed payment edges, 166 node features and 49 time steps. Following the temporal protocol established in earlier work, time steps 1 to 34 are used for fitting and steps 35 to 49 are held out. BitHGN reaches an illicit class F1 of 0.851 and an average precision of 0.879, compared with 0.788 for a tuned random forest and 0.812 for a heterogeneous graph transformer. The margin is widest after time step 43, where the closure of a large dark market changes the behaviour of the illicit population and every baseline degrades sharply. Ablation shows that relation typing contributes the largest single share of the improvement, followed by the imbalance aware objective. The model also degrades more gracefully than the homogeneous baselines under structural perturbation of the test subgraph, and its relation level attention weights produce an auditable account of why a given transaction was flagged. The results support the view that relation semantics, not just topology, carry a meaningful part of the laundering signal in Bitcoin.
why: Solid AML method but no deployment signals; benchmark, not operational ML.

title: Do LLM Screeners Share a Template? Auditing Surface-Feature Preferences in AI Resume and Loan Screening *
abstract: General-purpose large language models configured as application screeners can make similar decisions on the same inputs, but the observable features underlying that similarity are not well understood. We study seven screener configurations from four model families and two generations, on a synthetic resume corpus and, as a cross-domain comparison, on 800 human-written LendingClub loan narratives with repayment outcomes, estimating how each screener's decision depends on fourteen presentation and lexical features. On resumes, fitted feature-response indices are strongly correlated across screeners (cross-fitted correlations 0.84 to 0.96, all above a permutation benchmark of 0.72), with job-description vocabulary overlap among the most consistently weighted features. A paired rewrite experiment provides local causal evidence for this component: after excluding rewrites that a blinded audit identified as factually leaky or borderline, a keyword-mirroring intervention produced 10 selection flips against 1 reverse flip (+2.30 log-odds, p = 0.03). We detect no corresponding penalty from reducing overlap at the achieved dose, and formatting interventions with meaningful achieved doses yield estimates compatible with zero. The audit also carries a methodological warning: the unrestricted estimate (+3.89) is substantially larger than the audit-clean one, a gap consistent with unnoticed content drift in LLM-generated rewrites materially inflating estimated effects. On the LendingClub narratives, the same measured features explain substantially less variation in decisions and the fitted indices are unreliable, so the data do not support a generation-divergence interpretation of the cross-domain contrast; under the restricted lending information set, no screener's surface index is reliably associated with repayment, and approval rates vary from 42% to 86% on the same applications. These results identify a shared, keyword-sensitive component of LLM screening behavior under the studied conditions, and we release an audit protocol with simulation-calibrated operating characteristics for measuring such dependencies.
why: Good audit of LLM screener convergence but lending domain, not trading/execution.

title: Quantifying Sustainability for Structured Credit Products: An NLP-Driven ESG Scoring Approach
abstract: This paper develops an Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scoring methodology for structured credit products, with a particular focus on Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS). Conventional ESG frameworks are largely issuer-centric, whereas securitisations distribute economically relevant risks across originators, underwriters, servicers, trustees, borrowers and collateral. The proposed framework combines document-level natural language processing (NLP) for entity and role extraction with structured ESG information, role-based hierarchical weighting, and a news/controversy component. Zero-shot classification, transformer models (BERT/RoBERTa) and large language models are positioned as complementary tools for converting unstructured transaction documentation into an auditable entity-role representation. The methodology further incorporates entity resolution, parent mapping, confidence-aware data governance and temporal smoothing. A Freddie Mac Green Bond CMBS example illustrates the mechanics of the workflow and score decomposition. Numerical ESG and sentiment values in the case study are explicitly hypothetical placeholders; the application is a methodological demonstration rather than statistical validation. The contribution is therefore an instrument-aware, explainable architecture for sustainability assessment in structured credit, together with a research agenda for empirical calibration and cross-asset validation.
why: Solid ESG extraction via NLP/LLM but screening not execution or portfolio construction.

title: Topological Resolution Controlled Cross-domain Structural Evolution of RHIS across Regulatory, Contract, and Financial Transactions
abstract: Large language models can produce persuasive conclusions while leaving the structure of the underlying transaction implicit. This paper introduces topological resolution as a distinct property of an AI representation: under a fixed transaction, evidence cutoff, task, and output contract, it is the extent to which entangled information is separated into independent, typed, and addressable objects and relations. Topological resolution is explicitly separated from accuracy and completeness. We position RHIS as an external cognitive framework and runtime state machine for intelligent agents and examine its controlled structural evolution across four public-data studies-FTC Rytr, FTC Gateway, ContractNLI, and FIN-01-comprising 180 frozen outputs whose heterogeneous scores are not pooled. The LLM executed the assigned discovery and projection work autonomously inside fresh, controller-bound sessions; RHIS fixed the admissible sources, cutoff, schema, prior checkpoint, and claim boundaries, and no human drafted or corrected a response before freezing. In FIN-01, a five-case, four-arm financial-transaction lifecycle pilot, R1 produced a mean 116.73 typed topology objects and 34.93 relations across 15 paired case-by-cutoff units. Relative to B1, P1, and M0, R1 increased object counts by 158.3%, 38.5%, and 30.1%, and relation counts by 351.7%, 87.1%, and 65.3%, respectively; Holm-adjusted paired sign-flip p-values were at most .002197 for these two measures. All 45 relation-count contrasts favored R1. Forty of forty adjacent cutoff pairs were classified as formal topology jumps, so continuous manifold distances were withheld. These results support bounded claims of higher observed topological resolution, controller-governed autonomous LLM execution, and controlled cross-domain structural evolution. They do not establish semantic superiority, exhaustive reality reconstruction, or business utility.
why: Concept of topological resolution abstract; unclear method, no runnable path shown.

title: Beyond Delegation: Spillover Effects of Robo-Advisors on Investor Risk-Taking
abstract: As users delegate an increasing range of decisions to agentic information systems (IS) artifacts, little is known about whether the consequences of delegation remain confined to the delegated domain or spill over to decisions entirely under their control. We develop two competing perspectives. Under substitution, delegation reduces users' cognitive engagement and reliance on their own judgment, leaving the decisions they retain no better than before. Under empowerment, users learn from what the artifact does on their behalf, improving even the decisions that lie beyond the artifact's authority. We examine this question in retail investing, where investors delegate the management of part of their wealth to a robo-advisor while continuing to manage the rest in a separate self-managed account. Our data come from a proprietary investor-month panel from a leading robo-advisor ("Help You Invest") embedded in Alipay, covering both accounts of the same investors. We estimate a staggered difference-indifferences model that compares early adopters with matched late adopters, who serve as controls only in the months before they themselves adopt. The results favor empowerment. After the adoption of robo-advisors, investors hold more of their self-managed portfolio in risky assets, and a larger share of their purchases goes to risky funds. The composition of that risk also changes: portfolios become more exposed to broad market movements, less exposed to fund-specific volatility, and more widely spread across funds and asset classes. These shifts vary with platform membership tier, a predetermined measure of Ant-ecosystem activity and financial holdings: the move into risky assets is larger among lower-tier members, whereas the decline in fund-specific volatility is larger among higher-tier members. This study contributes to the literature on delegation to agentic IS artifacts and robo-advisors by showing that delegating portfolio management to robo-advisors can improve the risk-taking decisions made by investors alone.
why: Behavioral finance on delegation spillover but not about financial ML methods.

title: Maneuverability Under Reporting-Regime Uncertainty What to Do About AI Capital No One Records
abstract: Two organizations buy the same AI assistant in the same year, at the same price, for the same number of staff. One spends six weeks before launch writing down which cases the assistant may handle alone, assembling three hundred closed cases with known outcomes, recording who must approve which decisions, and logging the model version in force. The other sends an all-staff email with a training video. Their AI spending is the same number. Their financial statements are indistinguishable. No disclosure either is required to file today will separate them. When the provider replaces the model version, the first can re-run its cases and see what changed; the second finds out when staff start disagreeing with the output, or when a regulator asks how a decision was reached. This note takes up what a deploying organization should do about that while the reporting rules are unsettled. It is a companion to "The Economics of AI Capital Under Limited Observability" (v9.8, SSRN 7202978) and extends that framework to the reporting question. It reports no new evidence. Three arguments. First, the failure to record cuts both ways, and neither direction is a claim the underlying framework makes. That framework establishes an observability condition: where a configuration's composition cannot be recovered by inspection, or where its behavior can change with no human act, the record is the only access to what the object currently is. This note draws the reporting consequences. When such an arrangement decays, no required financial disclosure records the loss; when an organization builds capability it can stand behind, none records the gain. A third case is worse than either: a review step performed under load records an approval that the examination behind it did not support. The record is not silent but wrong, and cannot be checked by inspection because every field is properly filled. Second, the common framing of where this is heading is mistaken in both halves. Recognition is not moving — internally generated AI capability stays off the balance sheet. But IFRS 18, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, brings management-defined performance measures inside the audited financial statements. An organization publishing an AI-related performance measure will be audited on the management layer while nothing moves onto the balance sheet. The change arrives as a presentation standard rather than a recognition one, which is why it attracts little attention. Eight dated requirements across US and UK regimes are already in force or scheduled. Third, a small set of actions pays off under every outcome and is cheap now and impossible later. A record of which model version, which prompts, which data, which people and which permissions were in force in a given month can be made that month for the cost of an afternoon. It cannot be made two years later at any price. The note also introduces recomposition incidence: the location of the economic burden of a change to a productive arrangement, where that change is authored by one party and borne by another. Four features distinguish it from ordinary externality analysis — it is externally timed, unobservable to the bearer, recurring, and contractually normal. A closing section asks what follows if capability keeps compounding toward artificial general intelligence by way of self-improving systems. The capacity to establish what a system does divides into an automated part that gets cheaper as capability improves and a human part bounded by qualified judgment that does not. The scarce factor becomes qualified human judgment, and deployment into consequential decisions is bounded by establishment capacity rather than by capability. Ten labeled hypotheses are stated with the conditions that would falsify each. Three illustrations are drawn from published state government AI inventories, offered to show that the mechanism is observable in documents anyone can read rather than to establish a pattern from three cases.
why: Commentary on AI accounting uncertainty, not research study.

title: Forecasting ZMW/USD Volatility: Does the ZAR Volatility Framework Transfer to Zambia? A Comparative Study of GARCH, Stochastic Volatility, and Machine Learning Models in an Emerging Market Context
abstract: Accurate volatility forecasting for the Zambian Kwacha (ZMW) is critical for Bank of Zambia (BoZ) monetary policy, mining revenue hedging, and corporate risk management, yet ZMW remains severely under-studied despite high sensitivity to copper cycles and debt restructuring shocks. This paper transfers the framework from Mayambu (2026) SSRN 7029358 on ZAR/USD to ZMW/USD daily volatility from 2015 to 2026. We compare three modeling paradigms: classical GARCH/EGARCH, latent Stochastic Volatility (SV) estimated via MCMC, and machine learning approaches including LSTM and Random Forest. Using a rolling out-of-sample design from 2020-2026, we evaluate forecasts with MSE, QLIKE, and Diebold-Mariano tests.
why: Single currency transfer, standard models, limited scope.

title: Capital Heterogeneity, Shadow Credit, and Asymmetric Liquidation: Malinvestment in the Generative AI Infrastructure Boom
abstract: The rapid expansion of Generative AI (GenAI) infrastructure investment between 2023 and 2026 coincided with a severe contraction in commodity memory (DRAM) supply and a sharp rise in consumer hardware prices. Applying Austrian Capital Theory and an institutionally bounded extension of Austrian Business Cycle Theory (ABCT), this paper argues that the episode reflects genuine capital malinvestment rather than a transitory supply bottleneck: reallocating scarce 300mm silicon-wafer capacity toward High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is an unsustainable elongation of the structure of production. Because this boom occurred under a historically restrictive Federal Reserve policy rate, we decompose its financing into three tiers – an antecedent 2020–2022 monetary expansion that capitalized corporate and private-credit reserves, non-monetary federal semiconductor subsidy, and duration-transforming GPU-collateralized shadow credit – and state, tier by tier, the evidence that would falsify each. Grounding the analysis in the physical constraints of sub-micron 3D packaging, we show that the specialized equipment behind this reallocation is functionally non-convertible to commodity memory production even once its acquisition cost is written off in bankruptcy, though we bound this liquidation problem to its actual, modest share of aggregate AI infrastructure capital rather than letting it imply a macroeconomic weight the underlying capital layer does not carry. We reconcile the rapid 24–36 month obsolescence of AI-specific hardware with a slower, multi-year recovery of commodity memory supply, and bound all empirical claims to the memory and advanced-packaging segment of the 2023–2026 cycle.
why: Macro theory of AI-infra boom, on-topic to finance but not LLM/ML methods.

title: An Analytical Study of Generative AI in Finance: Evaluating Its Applications in Risk Modeling, Algorithmic Trading, Fraud Detection, and Ethical Challenges in Automated Decision-Making
abstract: This study analytically evaluates the transformative role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in financial services, focusing on its applications in risk modeling, algorithmic trading, fraud detection, and ethical implications in automated decisionmaking. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research integrates systematic literature review, quantitative simulations using real and synthetic datasets from 2022-2023, and qualitative ethical audits. Key findings demonstrate that GenAI-enhanced models achieve 25-35% improvements in risk simulation accuracy, 18% superior returns in algorithmic trading, and 98.5% fraud detection precision, while reducing false positives by 42%. However, ethical audits reveal persistent biases in automated lending (demographic parity = 0.09), underscoring transparency deficits. The study concludes that while GenAI drives $200-300 billion in annual banking value, robust governance frameworks are essential to mitigate systemic risks and ensure equitable outcomes. Policy recommendations include mandatory XAI audits and synthetic data standards.
why: GenAI survey with unsubstantiated claims, inflated numbers.

title: (PMF3) A Perspective on Modern Finance, with an AI View, Even toward CFO Roles: Part 3
abstract: "Modern Finance (MF)" apparently has a variety of definitions and/or connotations. Of concern is whether CFOs need to conform to any related "Modern Finance Theory (MFT)," even regarding what Artificial Intelligence (AI) might claim constitutes both MF and MFT. This paper begins an exploration of MF and MFT, in the context of roles of CFOs, even CFOs needing to address AI concerns as they express human intelligence (HI). Accordingly, this paper connects three questions. (1) What is modern finance and its theory? (2) What are roles of a CFO, especially regarding using (or not) modern finance and its theory? (3) What does generative-AI [as short for textual-generative-AI] say about modern finance, its theory, CFO roles, and CFO roles regarding modern finance and its theory? Where, naturally, this is merely an introductory exploration that raises more questions than it answers; yet in the process, explores the model validation process toward both AI and HI-even regarding an AI that may be swayed by the wrong HI. Where the main focus herein regards a model validation process toward content provided as AI-responses rather than the AI-process that provided such content.
why: Explicit position paper that 'raises more questions than it answers.'

title: Beyond the Scorecard: A Framework for Detecting False-positive Product-market Fit in Pre-seed and Seed-stage Ventures
abstract: Pre-seed and seed-stage capital allocation still relies on tools built for a pre-AI, single- region market. The Scorecard Method (Payne, 2001; revised 2019) and the TABS Score (2019) remain the most cited named frameworks in angel and early-stage due diligence, and neither was designed to separate self-reported founder enthusiasm from evidenced traction, nor to operate across the deal-structure differences that now separate North American SAFE-dominated pre-seed rounds from the Convertible Loan Agreements and Advance Subscription Agreements common in Europe, and the free-zone equity structures of the GCC. This gap has become material: seed-to- Series-A conversion for the 2022–2023 cohort fell to roughly 15%, down from over 30% for 2018–2020 cohorts, median time between seed and Series A has stretched toward 616 days, and 2026 investors are increasingly explicit about rejecting what they describe as “false positives” of product-market fit — traction signals that read as validation but do not survive institutional scrutiny. This paper introduces KVEX 10.1, an AI-orchestrated investability diagnostic that extends the KVEX v10.0 framework (Khan, 2026) with an explicit false-positive PMF detection layer, evidence-graded scoring, and a native regional adaptation model spanning North America, the GCC, and Europe. The framework is illustrated through three anonymized regional case applications — North America, GCC, and Europe — governed by NDA confidentiality protocol, in which a high-presentation traction claim (average self-reported presentation score of approximately 9.2/10 across the three cases) was in every case capped by a materially weaker evidence grade once verified, ranging from partial structural blockers to unverified self-reported pipeline. For founders, angels, and early- stage funds operating in a 2026 market the venture industry itself is calling a correction year after two years of hype-funded deals, this has direct implications for how investability should be assessed before capital changes hands. Version note: KVEX 10.1 (2026) extends v10.0 (Khan, 2026) by removing Modes 5 (PARTNERS) and 7 (VC FINDER), renumbering the remaining six modes, retaining the 12-factor investability diagnostic under the name Idea Validation Report, and confirming the regional adaptation layer for North America, GCC, and Europe.
why: Venture capital due diligence; off-domain from financial markets and trading ML.

title: They Lie and We Lie About the Lying: A Plain Language Account of Systematic Deception in Large Language Models and the Financial Incentives That Sustain It
abstract: Large language models lie. They produce false statements and present them as true. When users challenge these false statements, the models defend them. Only when confronted with undeniable evidence do they acknowledge error. The artificial intelligence industry has chosen to call this behavior "hallucination." This paper argues that the terminology itself is a form of deception, designed to make a fundamental flaw sound like an incidental quirk. The research literature has extensively documented that these systems are structurally incapable of reliably distinguishing truth from falsehood, that they are trained in ways that reward confident-sounding responses over accurate ones, and that they cannot verify their own outputs. This paper translates that research into language that does not require specialized training to understand. The goal is to make the problem visible to policymakers, educators, parents, and the general public who are being told these systems are ready for widespread deployment. The evidence shows they are not. The evidence has been available for years. The deployment continues because there is money in it.
why: Opinion essay on LLM deception; not research contribution or methodology.

title: Draft: Modelling Psychological and Cultural AI Risk Propagation in the Financial System
abstract: The financial system is a critical component of our society; its functioning determines the well-being of humans everywhere. The financial system is exposed to damage created by disruptive change which impacts its human components. One such change is the development of modern AI and modern AI's impact on human psychology and behaviours, and the knock on impacts on human institutions. The changes to human behaviour and institutions could potentially propagate into the functions of the financial system, changing and impairing them and creating significant harms. A specific example of this interaction (the suppression of human learning) is modelled as a computational simulation and a series of experiments using empirical data from recent real world measurements of AI impact on humans are reported. These indicate that the effects currently being measured and described in empirical studies of AI use and AI in education could create long term impairment of global system functions. Contribution: a description of how AI could impact the functioning of the financial system via psychological, cultural and institutional mechanisms; a description of an agent based simulation modelling institutional and global learning in the system based on data about the system in 2026 1 ; a demonstration of the impact of the empirical findings by David Stromberg et al. (2026) and Fabrizio Dell'Acqua et al. (2026) in the simulated system showing how significant long term harm to human knowledge systems emerges if the empirical information we have is correct and our modelling is appropriate. A result indicating that observed structures in the system are more robust to knowledge decay than synthetic structures, and another result is shown that demonstrates the negative impact of hiring freezes in response to AI. An effective mitigation of these effects could be the introduction of regulations mandating human capital control for financial services insituions.
why: Psychological risk propagation too speculative; no concrete method or evidence.

title: When AI Agents Buy the Ticket: The Impact of Agentic AI on Airline Pricing and Revenue Management
abstract: The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) may fundamentally change airline ticket purchasing by shifting sophisticated algorithmic decision making to the buyer side of the market. This study develops a simulation-based framework to examine how increasing AI-agent penetration affects airline demand allocation, price sensitivity of captured demand, revenue performance, and pricing decisions. Human travelers search restricted subsets of available alternatives, whereas AI agents systematically evaluate broader choice sets. The results show that agent-mediated search increases competitive transparency, amplifying both the benefits of attractive airline offers and the penalties associated with unattractive ones. These effects are not uniform across airlines or markets but depend on relative fares, schedule quality, competitive pricing, and market fragmentation across search sources. Importantly, greater AI penetration does not necessarily create uniform downward fare pressure; rather, it tends to compress sustainable fare differences. The findings suggest that airline responses to AI-mediated purchasing should depend on their competitive position and market environment.
why: Airline pricing; completely off-domain from financial markets.
